endorsements.quote: Co-frame the problem with patients, and where relevant, caregivers, before ‘success’ becomes fixed in a specification.

A minimal governance agenda for recognition-capable digital health would therefore include patient-defined value alongside clinical endpoints, transparency about intended use and trade-offs, post-deployment monitoring for inequitable impact and misrecognition, and stronger expectations around reporting and bias assessment when AI tools are introduced into care pathways.

unlisted_practices: Select patient-defined outcomes, including PROM domains that reflect lived burden, when designing and evaluating digital health and AI systems.
Preserve narrative channels such as free-text, diaries, and open prompts, and treat patients' and caregivers' interpretation as shared work.
Evaluate harms of misrecognition, such as labelling distress as non-compliance or disengagement as low motivation.
Interrogate proxies such as costs and utilization used in AI systems and test for inequitable impacts.
Assess patient-defined value alongside clinical endpoints rather than replacing clinical endpoints with PROMs.
Include caregivers in co-design and development of digital health tools.
